Name for the term: "Bể cá cộng đồng"
Name for the term: "community tank"
Name for the term: "Community aquarium"
A community tank holds several species of fish together rather than just one type.
Most community aquariums combine species that do not occur together in nature, chosen to match in temperament and water needs.
Community fish are usually peaceful species with similar environmental needs.
A community tank can be anything from beginner to advanced in difficulty, depending on the species chosen.
First gather the tank, stand, light, a filter sized for the tank, water conditioner, test kit, heater and thermometer, substrate and decor.
Rinse the tank, substrate and decor. Gravel may need several rinses.
Treat all water with conditioner before it goes into the tank.
Cycle the tank with the filter running for one to two weeks, testing the water daily, before adding fish.
Cycle the tank for about 2–6 weeks before adding fish, using starter bacteria or a small amount of fish food as an ammonia source.
Use a filter rated above the tank's volume, for example one rated 120–150 L for a 90 L tank.
Add fish in stages a few weeks apart: bottom fish and schooling fish first, Betta (Betta splendens) last.
Start with non-territorial, hardy species, and add more territorial fish after a few weeks.
Float the closed bag, mix tank water into it over time, then net the fish into the tank without pouring in the bag water.
Keep the lights dim for a few hours after adding new fish.
Quarantine new fish in a separate tank before adding them to an established aquarium, and acclimate them slowly to its temperature and water chemistry.
Plan where fish live, balancing species that swim at the top, middle and bottom of the tank.
One example combination: Neon Tetra (Paracheirodon innesi) in mid-water, in schools of 6–10 or more, with Panda Corydoras (Corydoras panda) on the bottom in groups of at least 6.
Most community species do well at a pH of about 6.5–7.5 and, for tropical species, 24–28°C.
Keep ammonia and nitrite at 0 ppm and nitrate below 20 ppm.
Most freshwater community fish need soft to moderately hard water with a pH of 6 to 8.
Ammonia is the most dangerous chemical in a community tank and should be tested for.
Changing 25% of the water each week keeps nitrate in check, provided the tank is not overcrowded.
Change 25–30% of the water each week and vacuum the gravel.
Test the water at least monthly, and more often in a new tank or if you are a beginner.
A general guideline is about 1 inch of adult fish per gallon. For example, a 10-gallon tank holds two schools of five fish under 1 inch.
TFH Magazine rejects the inch-per-gallon rule and says there are no good rules for maximum stocking. It advises watching waste, especially nitrate, instead.
The Hanoizoo article rejects the "1 cm per 1 L" rule. It says to size stocking by adult fish size, schooling needs, territoriality, bio-load and surface area.

Harlequin rasboras, cherry barbs and zebra danios do best in groups of six or more, though three to five of each is reasonable. A lone rasbora or cory is chronically stressed and more prone to disease.
Corydoras catfish are typical community fish, along with livebearers such as mollies (Poecilia) and platies (Xiphophorus), barbs, tetras, rasboras and danios.

Other suggested community species: Harlequin Rasbora (Trigonostigma heteromorpha), Otocinclus (Otocinclus affinis), Guppy (Poecilia reticulata), Molly (Poecilia sphenops) and Endler's livebearer (Poecilia wingei).
Cherry shrimp (Neocaridina davidi) help with algae in a community tank, but Betta (Betta splendens) may eat the young shrimp.
Betta (Betta splendens) can live with peaceful companions. Females or plakat types are suggested, because territorial males are the main risk.
Adding too many fish at once stresses them and causes dangerous swings in water quality.
Skipping the cycling period risks new tank syndrome.
Overcrowding leads to waste buildup, poor water quality and aggression.
Overstocking increases maintenance and makes the tank less able to cope with drops in oxygen.
Keeping aggressive or semi-aggressive fish in a beginner community tank is a mistake.
Pairing long-finned fish such as fancy guppies with fin-nippers such as tiger barbs is a common mistake.
Tiger barbs and serpae tetras may nip the fins of other fish.
Angelfish (Pterophyllum) eat very small fish, such as neon tetras and livebearer fry.
Mixing fish of very different sizes raises the risk of predation. Fish small enough to fit in another's mouth are at risk.
Unsuitable for community tanks: territorial or aggressive cichlids, predators such as snakeheads, leaffishes and bucktooth tetras, and large active fish such as tinfoil barbs and iridescent sharks.
Red-tailed black sharks should not be kept with others of their own species.
Choosing demanding species too early, such as discus, scarlet badis, licorice gouramis or mbuna cichlids, is a beginner's mistake.
Sharp gravel can cause infections in cory cats (Corydoras).
Do not buy fish that are lethargic or have sunken bellies, eroded fins or white spots.
Do not feed heavily on the first day.
Overfeeding raises ammonia and nitrate.
Do not clean all the filter media at once or rinse it in chlorinated tap water ("nước máy có Clo").
Do not mix saltwater and freshwater species.
Fish with different pH or hardness needs may not suit the same tank. Examples are cá trâm (pH 6.8–7.8) and cá neon (pH 6.0–7.0).
Peaceful community fish such as cá chuột and cá trâm should not be kept with large or aggressive fish, because some species nip fins and small, slow fish suffer.
Cá otto eat algae, so they need algae in the tank as food.
Vietnamese articles list cá chuột, cá neon, cá ember tetra, cá trâm, cá diếc anh đào, cá mún, cá bảy màu, cá otto, chạch culi and cá rìu vạch as gentle fish for a "bể cá cộng đồng".
Cá rìu vạch (family Gasteropelecidae) needs at least 75 lít for a group of 6.
Keep cá chuột and cá diếc anh đào in groups of at least 6, because they are shy when kept alone.
Cá mún and cá bảy màu breed readily, so a single pair can grow into a large group.
Temperature and size ranges given: cá neon 21–27°C, 3–5 cm; cá chuột 23–26°C, 4 cm; cá ember tetra 23–29°C, 2–3 cm; cá bảy màu 22–28°C, 4 cm.
Cá Cầu Vồng Việt (Melanotaenia praecox) grows to 6–8 cm and needs 23–28°C and pH 6.5–7.5. It shows its best colour in a group of 6 or more with several males.
Cá Hồng My needs a tank of at least 50 gallons and cooler water of 15–25°C.
Cá chuột lives on the bottom, so it complements mid-water and surface fish in a "bể cộng đồng".
In a Vietnamese forum thread on a discus tank with companion fish, a keeper said the companions pick up the discus's leftover food.
Keepers in the same thread warned that a large tank still needs regular water changes, and that uneaten food piles up on the bottom if it is not removed.
